cards.incumbent_reading: The paper holds that MCCL's firearms examiners kept their method because court challenges to firearms evidence were distant, while its toxicologists changed their reporting because a challenge was imminent in their own jurisdiction, so that locally immediate routes give more impetus to local change than remote ones (C03; F84, F87, F88, F160, F161, all in the author's voice).

wager.statement:
Re-attribute what separated the two units. The paper credits distance: remote for firearms, immediate for toxicology. A second thing varied across the pair and is printed on one side only: a change already being worked toward under a standing requirement.

Before the NAS report the laboratory was adapting to ISO 17025 and the toxicology unit had a multi-year plan to estimate measurement uncertainty (F98). State law and ASCLD required a five-percent confidence range for blood-alcohol measurement, the protocol already logged instruments, reagents and standards, and the laboratory was reporting at a 95% confidence level while preparing fuller uncertainty estimates for ISO compliance (F101). When the local challenge became imminent the unit accelerated that plan and prepared the statistical analysis (F98). At an outreach session for criminal-justice personnel Jason rejected the idea that the laboratory had only begun uncertainty work because of the NAS report, cited ISO and NIST requirements, and said the new calculation used several years of existing quality-control data (F102). The paper's own table puts ASCLD accreditation standards in toxicology's professional-association cell (F143, author's account) and identifies no professional-association route for firearms (F142, author's account).

On the firearms side no fragment prints a plan for the unit, and none says what the laboratory's ISO 17025 adaptation (F98) asked of it. The one professional-body response printed on the firearms criticism is a rebuttal: AFTE leaders issued a detailed rebuttal to parts of the NAS criticism of firearms work (F78). IAI and AFTE also answered the report with selected rebuttals and commitments to have their research committees study the recommendations further (F35). One examiner's work, at least, had been under outside review: Adam says outsiders had repeatedly reviewed his work without challenging it (F66).

Read this way, the pair does not set a unit that changed beside a unit that did not. It sets a unit whose change was already planned and required beside a unit with no plan and no requirement of its own in print, and the imminent challenge brought the plan forward. The wager is that the standing requirement is what made the difference, and that the immediate route accounts for when toxicology's reports changed, not for the fact that they did. A requirement met on a multi-year plan is hard to count among C03's locally immediate routes, so on this reading the pair shows the slower route doing the work.

This sits close to C17, which already lists accreditation work under way, and to F161, where the author's account has that work making the change easier. It parts from C03, which takes this pair to show that immediacy supplies the impetus.

what_it_would_take_to_cohere.observation: The timetable of the toxicology unit's multi-year plan as it stood before the local challenge, meaning when uncertainty estimates were due to enter reports, set against when they did; and whether the laboratory's ISO 17025 adaptation placed any requirement on the firearms unit.
what_it_would_take_to_cohere.basis: Not in the record. F98 prints that the plan was multi-year, predated the NAS report and was accelerated, but gives neither its original date nor how far it was brought forward. F101 and F102 print what the plan drew on, not when it was due. For firearms I read every fragment for that unit (F10, F14, F18, F22, F26, F29, F59 to F82, F84 to F87, F160, F171, and the Table 2 cells F130, F133, F136, F139, F142, F145, F148, F151), together with F83, a narcotics analyst speaking about firearms, F164 from the discussion, and the laboratory-wide fragments F36, F57 and F98. F98 has the laboratory adapting to ISO 17025 without saying what that asked of the firearms unit, no fragment prints a plan for firearms, and F142 records that the paper's table identifies no professional-association route for that unit. F33 and F34 print field-wide responses from AAFS and ASCLD without naming a unit. The corpus does not say why the timetable is not given.

strains_against: F98 -- two things in the stub that carries the reading. It prints that the unit accelerated the plan when the challenge became imminent, so immediacy can be moved from whether to when but stays in the episode and may have done more than the reading allows. And it has the laboratory, not the toxicology unit alone, adapting to ISO 17025 before the report; if that adaptation reached the firearms unit, that unit also stood under a requirement and did not change, and the variable the reading credits would not separate the two.

F90 -- a local defense attorney planned the challenge in an MCCL case and intended to bring in an outside engineering expert; the acceleration follows a concrete local event, which is the order C03 expects.

F81 -- the author's account is that the challenges to firearms evidence had not succeeded in excluding it, while F90 has the toxicology attack already winning DUI cases elsewhere; the record of the challenge also varied across the pair, and a challenge known to win could carry the difference without either distance or a standing requirement.

F103 -- the new reports state a narrow range at a 99% confidence level, where F101 has the laboratory previously reporting at 95%; if the plan did not already specify that level, the challenge shaped what changed as well as when, and the corpus does not say which.

F80 -- a firearms examiner who drew lessons from defense questioning urged colleagues to answer criticism and not dismiss it, and the author's gloss (p. 635) treats examiners with direct admissibility-hearing experience as more motivated toward field change; exposure moves at least what examiners say, where no plan or requirement is printed.

F153 -- outside the pair, narcotics had a professional-association route (F144, author's account) and is recorded as not changing; the reading holds only if what counted for toxicology was a requirement with a plan behind it (F98, F101), since the narcotics discussion is printed as considering a requirement (F124), not imposing one.

F33 -- AAFS and ASCLD supported the NAS recommendations and promoted actions such as universal laboratory accreditation and analyst certification; that is association pressure toward requirements on laboratories and analysts in general, the firearms unit not excepted.

F34 -- ASCLD advised laboratory leaders to ready staff for courtroom questions and to establish the reliability of their analyses; with F33, an association route to the firearms unit is in print in a general form, and the difference the reading credits narrows to whether a specific requirement and plan existed.

F67 -- firearms examiners contrast an earlier reliance on intuitive recognition with a current expectation of documented images; some change in how that unit backs its reports and testimony had happened by an undated point, so 'no plan in print' describes the record and may not describe the unit.
wager.who_could_complete_it: Whoever held the laboratory's accreditation timetable, such as unit supervisors, the laboratory director or the deputy director, or the laboratory's ISO 17025 planning documents from before the report, including whatever they asked of the firearms unit.

grounded_in.how: F98 prints a plan that predates the NAS report and was accelerated when the challenge became imminent; F88, in the author's voice, has the anticipated challenge creating the reason for toxicologists to change their reporting. One has the challenge altering the pace of a change already planned; the other has it supplying the reason for the change.

grounded_in.question: When was the multi-year plan due to put uncertainty estimates into reports, and how far did the imminent challenge bring that forward?
grounded_in.if_one_way: If the plan was due at about the time the reports did change, C03's toxicology case would read as a scheduled change that an immediate challenge barely moved, and the pair would not show immediacy producing change.
grounded_in.if_the_other: If the plan was years from delivery or had no reporting date, C03 would read as the paper states it: the immediate local route turned preparation into practice.

grounded_in.question: Did the laboratory's ISO 17025 adaptation (F98) place any requirement on the firearms unit?
grounded_in.if_one_way: If it placed a comparable requirement on firearms and that unit still did not change, C03 would read as stated, because the two units would then differ in the distance of their challenges and not in having a requirement.
grounded_in.if_the_other: If it asked nothing of firearms, C03's contrast would read as confounded: the units differed in whether any standing requirement existed, and distance could not be credited separately.

cards.rival: The paper's own account at full strength: a plan is not a practice. The unit accelerated and delivered once a challenge was planned in an MCCL case (F90, F98), and firearms, with no such case reaching local testimony (F84, author's account), changed nothing. The prior accreditation work lowered the cost, which C17 and F161 already say. On that reading the re-attribution is a shift of emphasis inside what the paper credits and is not needed.

cards.incumbent_reading: The paper holds that toxicologists and narcotics analysts each had an instrument-based route that could meet the comparison, and that toxicologists adapted because the demand fit their method and their error-avoidance values while narcotics analysts kept crystal testing because instrumentation threatened the variety, autonomy and craft they valued (C05, C18; F149, F150, F166, all in the author's voice).

wager.statement:
Re-attribute what separated the two units, from fit with what each values to how much of the unit's routine the change would displace and what that would cost.

On the toxicology side the change in print is to the report and the calculation behind it. Toxicology as the paper observed it was high-volume instrument work (F91). The protocol already logged instruments, reagents and standards, and the laboratory had been reporting at a 95% confidence level (F101). The courtroom attack was on reports that omitted measurement-uncertainty estimates (F90); the unit prepared the statistical analysis on a plan it already had (F98), and the new calculation used several years of existing quality-control data (F102). No fragment prints a change to how samples are prepared or run.

On the narcotics side what the analysts feared losing was the routine bench method: they feared their working group might eventually prohibit crystal testing (F121). Crystal tests handled many routine cases and often confirmed common methamphetamine in about ten to fifteen minutes, GC/MS was reserved for unknown or unconfirmed substances, and rapid legal turnaround made the faster method especially useful (F109). Robin said the laboratory could not handle its caseload without crystals because it had only two relevant instruments and instrument runs took too long (F123). Jodi expected a shift toward slower GC/MS if crystal testing were phased out (F122). The analysts said a rule of independent visual confirmation would in effect require a fresh duplicate test and roughly double the work (F124), and they noted that microscope cameras would cost less than additional GC/MS instruments (F125).

So the two instrument-based routes the pair holds comparable are not the same size of thing. For toxicology the instrument method was the routine and the demand added a calculation to it. For narcotics the instrument method was the exception, and what the analysts feared would have put it in place of the routine. The wager is that this difference, in how much of the day's work is displaced and what that costs in instruments and time against the caseload, is what made the units come out differently, and that the values the paper credits accompany each outcome without being shown to produce it.

Two things in print lean this way. The narcotics analysts' stated reasons divide: time, work and cost in F122, F123, F124 and F125; variety and what the work asks of the analyst in F127 and F128. That they were especially troubled by the second kind is the author's account (F126). And on the toxicology side the participant fragments show vigilance against sample-identity and pipetting mistakes (F94, F95, F96); the fit between that and estimating uncertainty across equipment, reagents and procedural steps (F102) is made in the author's voice (F100, F149), and the nearest participant-side item is pride shown when the new reports were presented (F103), which comes after the change.

The reading is close to the paper in one respect: the paper's own account of narcotics values includes quick case completion (F111, F120, author's account), so speed is registered. It parts from the paper in treating instruments, run time and caseload as conditions of the laboratory, not as something the analysts value, and in crediting them for the outcome where C18 credits variety, autonomy and craft judgment.

what_it_would_take_to_cohere.observation: An occasion on which cost and craft come apart for the narcotics analysts, either the instrument route offered without the limit in instruments and run time, or a change that keeps crystal testing while adding work, together with what the analysts then did.
what_it_would_take_to_cohere.basis: Not in the record as an action. F124 comes nearest: a confirmation rule under discussion that would keep crystal testing, to which the analysts' printed response is that it would roughly double the work; but that is talk about a proposal, and no fragment prints what was done. F125 prints the cameras as discussed, not as acquired. Nothing in F106, F109, F121 to F128 or F147 prints the instrument route on terms free of the limit Robin describes in F123. On the toxicology side nothing in F88 to F104 prints a demand that would have replaced the bench method.

strains_against: F128 -- Billie's stated reason for preferring crystal tests is that they let her practice chemistry and vary her work, and that loading drugs onto one instrument over and over would be intolerably monotonous; nothing in it concerns caseload, instruments or cost.

F127 -- Taylor's objection is that instrument operation could be done by almost anyone while crystal work takes validation and specialized training; that is about what the work asks of the analyst, not about what the laboratory can run.

F114 -- Taylor recounts taking a toxicology job, disliking its paperwork-heavy routine and persuading management to train him for other work; an analyst is printed acting on a preference about the work itself.

F113 -- narcotics analysts set their own craft-oriented chemistry against toxicology, which they describe as repetitive instrument work with little variety; the preference is voiced with no reference to caseload, instruments or cost, as is the excitement over unusual items in F112.

F98 -- the toxicology unit's plan for uncertainty estimates was multi-year and was accelerated only when the local challenge became imminent; a change that sat on a multi-year plan until a challenge brought it forward is not obviously a small one, and the pair also differs in that narcotics is printed with no such challenge (F162, author's account).

F103 -- the toxicologists appeared proud of a narrow range at a 99% confidence level, and F31 has them enthusiastic about the new reporting practice; pride in the figure suits the paper's account of a demand that fit them at least as well as it suits a change that was merely small.
F102 -- the calculation assessed uncertainty across equipment, reagents and procedural steps; how much work that was is not printed, so 'small' is the reading's estimate and not a printed fact.

F119 -- analysts pressing an IT representative to cut data-entry delays, with Billie joking that even an entry time close to the previous system's was too slow, shows speed pursued as something they care about, which is how the paper codes it; on that showing the time-and-work statements could be statements of value and the re-attribution a relabelling.

F71 -- outside the pair, all three qualified firearms examiners knew a counting method (F171) and did not routinely use it, on the printed ground that their broader visual judgments were more conservative (also F73); a change with no printed cost in instruments is not taken up, for a reason that is not about cost.
wager.who_could_complete_it: Narcotics analysts asked what they would choose with instruments and run time not limiting; the laboratory's instrument and caseload records; any record of whether cameras or further instruments were acquired.

grounded_in.how: Robin's printed reason for keeping crystals is caseload against two instruments and long runs (F123). The author's account is that analysts were especially troubled by the loss of autonomy, variety and judgment (F126). The stated reasons in print divide between the two kinds (F122, F123, F124, F125 against F127, F128); the ranking between them is the author's.

F94 has the toxicologists stressing the prevention of sample-identity mistakes by checking lists and labels; F149, in the author's voice, has measurement-error practices fitting the unit's commitment to avoiding mistakes. The participant fragment concerns specimens kept straight as they move through the process; the author's cell extends that commitment to estimating the uncertainty of a measurement.

grounded_in.question: Does any toxicologist, in print, connect the uncertainty estimate to the unit's concern with avoiding mistakes?
grounded_in.if_one_way: If the paper had printed a toxicologist making that connection, C05 would read on the toxicology side as the participants' own filter at work, and the pair would set a fit with values beside a conflict with values, as the paper has it.
grounded_in.if_the_other: If none made it, or the only printed account ran through ISO, NIST and existing data as F102 does, C05's toxicology side would read as the author's inference, and the pair would set a small addition beside a large substitution.

grounded_in.question: Were the microscope cameras discussed in F125 acquired?
grounded_in.if_one_way: If they were, C18 would read as a unit that changed how its results are kept for later review by the cheaper route in print while keeping its method, a local change of the kind toxicology made.
grounded_in.if_the_other: If they were not, which is the way F153's record of no local change leans although no stub prints what became of the discussion, C18 would read as stated: crystal-testing practices retained and no local change.

cards.rival: The paper's own account makes quick case completion one of the things narcotics analysts value (F111, F120, author's account; F119), and C20 holds that values grow out of what the work requires. On that reading the caseload and run-time statements are statements of value, C05 already covers them, and nothing needs re-attributing; the pathway difference the paper credits elsewhere, no immediate compulsion for narcotics (C18; F162, author's account), does the rest.

cards.trigger: unresolved_question_gaps DG02, which bears on ventured claim C19 (the entry also lists ventured claims C09, C22, C23)
cards.incumbent_reading: The paper ventures that spillovers reach occupations sharing evaluating audiences and overlapping activities, treats firearms, toxicology and narcotics as three neighbors the DNA comparison reached, and leaves open only how far beyond them it extends (C19, DG02; F165, author's account).

wager.statement:
Read the ending as provisional at its near edge as well as its far one. The paper closes with three units inside the comparison's reach and the outer boundary unknown (F165, author's account). In print the three do not sit inside it in the same way.

Firearms: the NAS report says techniques such as toolmark comparison had not received stringent testing, lacked known error rates and had produced some erroneous results when compared with DNA evidence (F60); a SWG-GUN board member says attempts to exclude firearms evidence were becoming more common (F62); an examiner at the statewide meeting says firearms work could not simply be made equivalent to DNA analysis (F82). Narcotics: an analyst describes the demand on non-DNA specialties as pressure to become more like DNA analysis (F41), and Jodi fears crystal testing could be phased out because it leaves no persistent instrument output for later review (F122); the participant link to DNA on this side is F41 alone, and it is stated for non-DNA specialties in general. Toxicology: the report did not criticize toxicology directly (F89); the uncertainty plan predates the report (F98); the requirements named are ISO, NIST, state law and ASCLD (F101, F102); the courtroom attack is on reports that omit uncertainty estimates (F90); and Jason rejects the idea that the laboratory had only begun the work because of the report (F102). No toxicology stub has a toxicologist, or the attorney, naming DNA. That toxicologists encountered the DNA comparison through that case is the author's account (F99, F131, F157).

The wager: the edge that DG02 looks for beyond the three may run between them, with toxicology, the one unit recorded as changing its practice (F152, author's account), on the far side. If so, the sorter ventured in C19 does not find the edge, because the three units share a laboratory, a director who says all are criminalists who should be capable of working in any unit (F57), and, on the paper's account, their audiences (F165). The ending would also change shape: the comparison reached two units and, on the paper's own record, changed local practice in neither (F151, F153, author's account), while the unit that changed did so under requirements and a courtroom strategy whose tie to DNA is printed only in the author's voice.

The far edge is no better fixed. The only named forensic occupation in print beyond the three and DNA is the trace examiners, whose flyer said trace work had been pushed behind DNA work and whose printed concern is attention and resources (F55); no stub has their methods evaluated against DNA's.

what_it_would_take_to_cohere.observation: Words from a toxicologist, or from the attorney behind the uncertainty challenge, naming DNA or the 2009 report as the standard being applied to toxicology reports; or the challenge's own terms, showing where its demand for uncertainty estimates came from.
what_it_would_take_to_cohere.basis: Not in the record. I read every toxicology fragment (F11, F15, F19, F23, F25, F31, F88, F89, F91 to F104, F161, and the Table 2 cells F131, F134, F137, F140, F143, F146, F149, F152) and F90, the one fragment on the defense strategy. F90 prints what the attack targets and that it had won cases elsewhere, not where its demand came from. F102 is the only place a toxicologist is printed speaking of the report, and there he rejects it as the origin of the work. The link to DNA is made in the author's voice in F99, F131 and F157.

strains_against: F102 -- the idea Jason rejects is printed as an idea in play at the outreach session, that the laboratory had only begun the work because of the report; and 'only begun' leaves room for the report having mattered to how the work went on.

F89 -- the same stub that says the report did not criticize toxicology directly says it emphasized assessing accuracy and estimating error rates, which matches the content of the attack in F90; a match of content is what the paper's reading expects.

F33 -- AAFS and ASCLD answered the report by supporting its recommendations and promoting actions such as universal laboratory accreditation; through those bodies the report is printed as reaching laboratories in general.

F34 -- ASCLD's response to the report advised laboratory leaders to ready staff for courtroom questions and to establish the reliability of their analyses; with F101 placing ASCLD among toxicology's standing requirements, the report has a printed route to every unit through that body.

F36 -- MCCL management circulated the report summary and instructed staff to read the full document; the report reached every unit as required reading, so the reading has to hold that being told to read it differs from having one's own practice measured by it, a distinction that is the reading's and not the paper's.
F41 -- a narcotics analyst describes the demand as falling on non-DNA specialties in general, toxicology not excepted.

F54 -- members of non-DNA units, units not named, repeatedly compared their resources with forensic biology's; if toxicologists were among them, a comparison with DNA is voiced in that unit after all, though about equipment, money and staffing.

F123 -- Robin describes a workshop about a Daubert challenge to crystal testing; the stub does not say what kind of challenge that is or where it arose, but a challenge to a method the report is not printed as criticizing is the subject of a workshop, so challenges are not confined to what the report named, which weakens the ground for placing toxicology outside the reach.

cards.rival: The paper's own: the report's emphasis on estimating error rates (F89) is the comparison as it applies to a quantitative method, the uncertainty challenge (F90) is that emphasis arriving by court, and a participant's denial that the report started the work (F102) is compatible with the report having made it urgent. On that reading toxicology is inside the reach and the edge is where DG02 puts it, somewhere beyond the three.

cards.incumbent_reading: The paper uses the forensic biology unit as the benchmark: statistical conventions, review and reviewable outputs make a messy, judgment-heavy process look objective to outsiders (C14), and that standing is what the other units are compared against (C02).

wager.statement:
Retold from the forensic biology unit's own fragments, the paper's episode has no event in it. None of the unit's fourteen fragments has a DNA analyst speak of the 2009 report, of being the standard, or of the other units; the nearest is the supervisors introducing themselves, as a joke, on the author's first day, as the 'DNA princesses' (F28). What the fragments do carry is the unit's account of its own work and one line of history.

At the bench the analysts regard profiling as judgment-laden and untidy, because instrument output can contain artifacts and samples can be dirty, degraded or contaminated (F48). Terri describes a contaminated saliva control that cleared when she repeated the amplification, and Carly says contamination can persist with no identifiable cause (F49). In the paper's description, conclusions often took repeated interpretation and discussion between analyst and reviewer, sometimes with others brought in (F50), and Terri remarks that writing a report could take the wider laboratory (F51). What goes out is a profile released after technical and administrative review (F45) and a report that pairs a contributor conclusion with a population-frequency figure (F46). And the method became established over roughly twenty-five years, after technical advances, court challenges and favorable National Academy assessments in the 1990s (F43, which the paper draws from cited sources).

The wager from this side: the forensic biology unit is not the fixed point the other three are measured from but one more unit whose work is judgment talked through with a reviewer, and whose occupation was itself under court challenge and Academy assessment first. The firearms review in F69, two examiners debating how much agreement is enough, is the nearest printed counterpart to F50. Review of an analyst's work by someone else is printed for every unit (F45 with F50, F68, F92, F110); what is printed for forensic biology alone is the population-frequency figure (F46). If so, what each neighbor is compared with (C13) and found compatible or incompatible with (C04; F145, F146, F147, author's account) is what leaves the DNA unit, and the judgment that the paper's table sets against the objectivity associated with DNA (F148, author's account) is present on the DNA side as well (F48).

This agrees with the paper on the substance of C14, untidy work and outputs that look objective, and uses the same fragments. It differs in where it puts the unit: among the cases, with a history of being evaluated, and not above them. Whether the review steps and the figure are what that earlier evaluation left behind is not printed, and the reading does not assert it.

what_it_would_take_to_cohere.observation: What the forensic biology analysts said or did about being the standard, to the other units, to legal audiences, or about the report that exempted their work; and whether the review steps and the frequency figure were in place before the court challenges and assessments that F43 records or were taken on in their course.
what_it_would_take_to_cohere.basis: Not in the record. Of the unit's fourteen fragments (F07, F09, F13, F17, F21, F28, F43, F45, F46, F47, F48, F49, F50, F51) only F28 has DNA staff refer to themselves as a group, and it is a joke on the author's first day. F43 gives the sequence of advances, challenges and assessments without saying what the occupation or the unit changed along the way. F36 has management instruct staff to read the report and prints no reaction from this unit. F54 and F55 print what others say about DNA's resources, not what the DNA unit says back.

strains_against: F60 -- the report states that techniques such as toolmark comparison had produced some erroneous results when compared with DNA evidence in the same cases; there DNA evidence is what the others are found wrong against, a standing above the other cases that the analysts' view of their own bench work (F48) does not remove.

F49 -- the incident involves a control sample and an amplification that was repeated, after which the problem was gone; the judgment here is exercised over a step that can be run again, and no counterpart to that is printed in the firearms review of F69, so the two kinds of work may be less alike than the reading needs.

F46 -- the population-frequency calculation is a step of the work as well as a feature of the report, as is assigning alleles across sixteen loci in F45; the line between the bench and what leaves the unit is the reading's, and these two stubs sit across it.

F86 -- the MCCL firearms examiners held that a DNA-like statistical population made little sense for firearm marks; they treat the figure as something their evidence cannot have, which makes the difference one of the evidence and not only of what is handed outward.
F43 -- the same stub lists technical advances and favorable assessments; the standing may have been earned by the technique, as the paper's account has it, with nothing left behind by the challenges.
F28 -- a joke on a first day may carry no view of the unit's standing; the stub prints no explanation, and the reading cannot lean on it.
wager.who_could_complete_it: Analysts and supervisors of the forensic biology unit speaking about the comparison; the unit's own procedural history, meaning when its review steps and its statistical reporting were introduced.

grounded_in.question: Did the forensic biology analysts, anywhere in print, speak about being the standard, either putting it forward before neighbors or legal audiences or disowning it?
grounded_in.if_one_way: If they are printed putting it forward, C13 would read with the benchmark partly kept up by the benchmark unit itself, and the features the neighbors select would be features DNA analysts advance.
grounded_in.if_the_other: If they are printed disowning it, as F48 leans, C13 would read with the neighbors selecting features of what leaves the DNA unit that its own analysts do not claim for the work.

grounded_in.question: Were the technical and administrative review (F45) and the population-frequency figure (F46) in place before the court challenges and Academy assessments of F43, or adopted in their course?
grounded_in.if_one_way: If in place before, C02 would read as stated: a technique whose own features carried it to benchmark standing, after which evaluation turned on the neighbors.
grounded_in.if_the_other: If adopted in their course, C02 would read with DNA as an earlier recipient of the same evaluation, and the benchmark as what that evaluation left in one occupation's practice.

grounded_in.how: F48 has the DNA analysts regard their own profiling as judgment-laden and untidy; F148, in the author's voice, sets the objectivity associated with DNA against firearms' commitment to trained subjective judgment. The first puts judgment inside DNA work; the second places DNA across the line from judgment. The paper marks the same gap itself at F52; the reading uses it against the table's compatibility cells and not only under C14.

cards.rival: The paper's own placing of the unit: C14 already says DNA work is messy and its outputs look objective, and C13 already says neighbors take up selected features. On that reading the unit's history (F43) is background and its bench talk is the point C14 makes; putting the unit among the cases adds nothing, because what bears on the neighbors is how courts, media and the public treat DNA (F52, author's account), whatever DNA analysts think of their own work.

declined.trigger: ventured_claims C09, C22, C23 (listed in the same entry as DG02; no separate reading written)
declined.why: The dossier (section 7) says only an unresolved-question gap parameterises this move, so the entry's one reading is written on DG02 and the claim it bears on, C19. C22 and C23 have no fragments beneath them and concern settings outside the laboratory (ethnographers' masking practices, digital technologies); nothing printed could be used differently, and a reading would be restatement or import. The fragments beneath C09 (F47, F52, F53) are all in the author's voice, so no printed event sits beneath the claim; the one stub bearing on how DNA came by its standing, F43, belongs to the forensic biology unit's fragments and is taken up in the focalization reading.
